newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-Fitzy targeted for "special treatment".
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-Fitzy targeted for "special treatment".

text.p: DUNEDIN, Aug 18 NZPA - All Black captain Sean Fitzpatrick has been a victim of some brutal attacks in test rugby this season.
The series of assaults on him in the last couple of months is proof that he had been singled out for special treatment by the Springboks and the Wallabies.

But the highly competitive front rower has always been at pains to answer queries regarding such subjects, believing on-field incidents should remain within the bounds of the corner flags, and if officials felt further action was needed then it was up to them.

However, the 34-year-old hooker hinted yesterday that he believed he had been targeted in the Bledisloe Cup and Tri-Series, both retained by the All Blacks, after a punch on his face by Wallaby No 8 Troy Coker at Carisbrook on Saturday.
The All Blacks won the trans-Tasman clash 36-24.

Fitzpatrick required immediate medical attention and Coker was penalised, warned and later cited for punching. The offence, however, merits a sending off let alone a yellow card in the Tri-Series. French referee Joel Dume administered neither.

The Sanzar judicial committee that heard Coker's case, said he did not punch, as charged by an independent South African citing commissioner, and accepted his explanation that it was part of a clearing movement. Coker went off free.
However, video replays clearly show that Coker struck the All Black hooker on the face, turned sideways, with an intentional right-hand swing when Fitzpatrick was locked upright in a ruck.
"No, I don't think so," Fitzpatrick said when asked if he believed another player would have received the same treatment had he been in the captain's situation on Saturday.
"Do you think you have been targeted?" he was asked.
"Maybe," he responded.
After a previous similar attack on him a week earlier, his answer was: "No, I don't think so," when asked if he was being singled out.
Fitzpatrick, nevertheless, shook his head in disbelief when told of the judicial committee's decision.
"Well, these things happen," was all that he was prepared to say.

Australian and South African players, and it appears that referees too, have shown little sympathy for the most-capped (92 tests) All Black whenever they've found him even slightly off the line this year.
His treatment appears to be the result of his reputation of being a hard player, who uses provocation and annoyance with great subtlety.

But the attacks on him by Coker, a week earlier by Springbok Andre Venter and before that by Wallaby captain John Eales, were brutal and bordered on cowardly acts as Fitzpatrick had been genuinely pinned on either offside positions or on the ground
and defenceless.
Worse still was the fact that in all the cases he wasn't expecting them and was looking in a different direction.
He was vigorously rucked at Ellis Park, accepted it graciously for being offside accidentally, and punched twice by Australian captain John Eales at the MCG. Eales was lucky to remain on the field.

South African Andre Venter was sent off at Eden Park for stomping Fitzpatrick's face when he was caught on the wrong side of a ruck, which had gone forward. Venter was later suspended for three weeks for the ugly foul, which could have caused
severe damage had Fitzpatrick not cushioned the blows.
Other players who have had a go at him this season include Springbok Andre Snyman and Wallabies James Holbeck and Ben Tune.
The attacks on Fitzpatrick are neither surprising nor new, for his rugby deeds may win him a knighthood but highly unlikely a sainthood.

But what has been surprising has been the attackers' disregard of the consequences to their own team if they were marched from the field, and a tendency by referees not to take the offences against Fitzpatrick as seriously as they would normally do with the other players.
